idiom_name: requestAnimationFrame(time => ...) frame callback with a lag accumulator
implementation_notes: The browser event loop owns the cadence: requestAnimationFrame 'requests the browser to call a user-supplied callback function before the next repaint', with call frequency generally matching the display refresh rate, and the callback receives a DOMHighResTimeStamp 'indicating the end time of the previous frame's rendering'. What replaces the classic structure: the callback re-arms itself - rAF is one-shot, and MDN states that the callback 'must call requestAnimationFrame() again if you want to animate another frame' - while a lag accumulator turns timestamp deltas into fixed steps, so the loop body is the callback. MDN's warning is the pattern's core discipline: always compute progress from the timestamp argument, 'otherwise, the animation will run faster on high refresh-rate screens'. Callbacks pause in background tabs, so clamp accumulated time before stepping.
pitfalls: rAF is one-shot: forgetting the re-arm stops the loop silently, and an exception thrown inside the callback also stops it because the next request never runs - re-arm before doing the frame's work.

Timestamp precision is deliberately coarsened (5 microseconds in cross-origin-isolated contexts, 100 microseconds otherwise per MDN); do not assume sub-millisecond accuracy or stable inter-frame deltas.
Callbacks pause in background tabs and hidden iframes, so minutes of wall time can accumulate before the next frame - clamp before stepping or the simulation teleports.
A 120 or 144 Hz display fires more often than 60 Hz: per-callback deltas make motion speed follow the monitor, while the accumulator keeps simulation time independent of refresh rate.

variants.name: Node.js manual loop with timers and a monotonic clock
variants.implementation_notes: Node has no frame callback; its timer functions 'implement a similar API as the timers API provided by Web Browsers but use a different internal implementation that is built around the Node.js Event Loop'. What replaces the classic structure: hand-write the driver - a recursive setTimeout (or setImmediate) re-arms the loop, performance.now() supplies a monotonic timestamp for the accumulator, and the requested delay is only a pacing hint because timers fire late and never early. Use setImmediate for 'as fast as the event loop allows' and setTimeout for a target rate; either way clamp accumulated lag so a busy event loop cannot spiral. This is the headless/server shape of the pattern: authoritative game servers, tick loops and simulations.
pitfalls: setTimeout on a busy event loop fires late; never use the requested delay as the elapsed time - measure with performance.now() and clamp.
Timers are not a fixed-step source: callback cadence drifts with the event loop's phases, so counting callbacks diverges from real time.
An exception thrown inside the callback breaks the recursion and stops the loop; re-arm before doing work or wrap the body in try/finally.
